Swoop is live in Nigeria, starting in Yaba. We’re excited to announce our $7.3M seed round, led by Long Journey , Variant, Version One Ventures , Dune Ventures , and Soma Capital , with participation from Zero Knowledge Ventures , Walter Kortschak , Basecapital.io , and others. We’re putting that capital behind a simple goal: make food delivery in Lagos more affordable. Our pricing model is simple. 100% of your delivery fee goes to the rider, and we charge a small 7% service fee to keep the lights on. Lagos alone has 20M+ people and a food economy growing faster than almost anywhere on the planet. The opportunity is massive, but so is the gap in service. We’re excited to help close it, beginning in Yaba. If you're interested in working with us, send us a DM.

This past weekend, I competed in my first-ever hackathon — the GStack x GBrain Hackathon hosted at Y Combinator . My teammate Nicolas Vega and I built an AI-native educational platform using GStack and GBrain that adapts to your learning level in real time. We walked away with 2nd place, which caught me completely off guard! A little about me: I'm a first-gen rising junior at UC Berkeley studying CS. Access has been the thread through everything I've done/built. Growing up in a city that was constantly ranked top 3 most dangerous cities in California, opportunities like this didn't come to you — you had to go find them. That shaped how I think about building. Last year, I co-founded Swoop , a food delivery platform in Eswatini that grew to 20,000+ users in under two months and has since raised ~$7M to expand to Nigeria and become Africa's first super-app. The infrastructure people take for granted in other countries didn't exist, so we built it. I stepped away to come back to school. Now I'm working on something new — building an AI consumer product for the millions of people who've never been "looped" into the tech world and the ones who don't have access to what AI can do for them. Still early, but the problem is real and I'm working on it every day. This hackathon was an incredible introduction to the space. Being in a room full of builders at YC, shipping something under pressure with someone I'd just teamed up with last-minute, reminded me why I love this. I look forward to competing in more. Congrats to Sina Matian on taking 1st place, well deserved! This is my first LinkedIn post. If you're building, learning, or just figuring it out — I'd love to connect. Huge thanks to Garry Tan , James Tan , and the GBrain team for putting this together. Shoutout to the sponsors: The Hog (YC F25) , ZeroEntropy , jo (YC W24) , Transpose Platform , Lightsprint (YC P26) , gbrain.io , and the Y Combinator team.

Today, we launched Swoop 's WhatsApp ordering service in Lagos. Food delivery apps in Nigeria are continuing to grow over 100% every year. Within 3 years, most food delivery orders in Nigeria will be placed by people who are not currently using food delivery. Our WhatsApp ordering service is another step towards being the easiest and best destination for these new customers. This means delivering a seamless, shockingly fast version of the process that these customers are already familiar with. Thousands of Lagosians already order goods online through WhatsApp every day. The process is familiar, but customers lose time sharing delivery details, checking availability, and confirming payment. Swoop makes the entire process faster. Text “hi,” choose a restaurant, place your order, and let Lagos’s fastest delivery network handle the rest. The goal of this feature is simple: make Swoop the easiest place for Nigeria’s next generation of digital customers to order online.

a bit late but i went to YC startup school... pretty fun time, and another excuse to go to SF. some notes: demographics: - lots of highschoolers from around the US. i didn't even know about startups in high school. age floor is ~middle school. - ran into a bunch of my buddies from around the US (didn't know they were coming), and also made a bunch of friends from various colleges. - spent a lot of time with a few people I met, instead of broad networking (as one should at large networking events). shoutout Jason Li , Samuel Liu , Leo Yang and many others. event specifics: - most talks were useless, as expected. Jensen's was the best, mainly bc he talked a lot about management/leadership tech instead of the newest Claude feature or AI paradigm. Waymo CEO talk also good because it was technical and about the self driving stack. - afterparties were the funnest part; free food, small group networking. chose a few that fit my interests the best (so not all the AI infra companies...) - spent a bunch of time walking around SF parks w/ friends instead of listening to talks on AI policy, etc. weather was quite warm. what could have been improved: - venue was great, lots of free snacks, but I would have had more conference rooms and scrap silent disco style workshops. - they only had 2 companies doing demos outside--would have loved to talk to more founders about company culture, why they are motivated, background, etc. - there was too many people, a lot of kids were there just for the AI credits, they didn't even seem excited to see big names in person?? overall great weekend. i made a bunch of friends and would def go next year.

Everyone is using AI to code, but most developers are still spending hours reviewing the output and reprompting models to fix the same minor issues over and over again. The biggest gain with AI should not just be generating code faster; it should be drastically reducing the time you spend reviewing it before anything ships. That’s why we built Agentic IDE Inc. Instead of catching the same problems in review every sprint, our infrastructure encodes the rules for how things get implemented before your agent ever starts working, so you get quality code the first time rather than spending hours undoing what AI introduced. Today we are launching Plan Mode, and here is a look at what is making this possible: Containerized Knowledge Profiles allow you to swap knowledge layers in under 30 seconds using automatic skills backed by semantic, relational, and graph storage that accurately model human reasoning across your entire codebase. Skill Audits Prior to Execution mean that before your agent writes a single line of code, our harness automatically finds and injects your team's most relevant rules into context, catching things like silent retries where it should fail hard before they ever make it into review. Autonomous Agent Fleets connect to a shared brain profile to take on parallel jobs simultaneously, letting your team execute complex tasks at a speed that simply was not possible before. Nobody has built a production-quality gate for AI harnesses until now, and we want to help teams stop reviewing AI slop and start shipping code they can actually stand behind. If you are ready to cut your refactor and review time by hours, try Plan Mode at aideapp.dev and reach out if you want to bring it to your team.

A food delivery app is only as good as the people behind every order. Before an order gets to a customer in perfect condition, there’s a lot that happens behind the scenes to make that possible. - From the vendors preparing and packaging every meal. - The riders who brave the sun and the rain to deliver it. - And the customers who trust us with their orders. Every delivery is made possible by people. We believe those stories deserve to be told because stories help us see the people behind the service. They remind us that behind every order is someone working hard to make someone else’s day a little easier. That’s why we created People Who Swoop—a series that shines a light on the people who make Swoop what it is. Every episode tells the story of the people behind the brand, why they do what they do, and gives us all the opportunity to see the job from a different perspective. Our first episode follows Idris, one of our top-performing riders, through a typical day on the road. We also had a little surprise waiting for him at the end. 💜

The most hurtful thing an investor ever said to me was, “You should just get a job.” I’m sure he meant it as genuine advice, and having met so many founders, he probably saw that I wasn’t founder material. And he was probably right. I’m not naturally well-spoken, charismatic, decisive, or even particularly opinionated. But growing up as the shortest, weakest, and shyest person among my peers, I learned that who I am does not define what I do. “You can’t play sports because you’re short.” “You can’t speak in public because you’re shy.” “You can’t lead because you’re awkward.” I believe the second half of every one of those statements. But not the first. Not because I want to prove anything, but because what I want to pursue simply isn’t what I’m naturally good at. And that’s okay. There is wisdom in playing to my strengths, but I choose to believe in the courage it takes not to back down from my weaknesses.

Swoop just raised $7.3 million to launch food delivery in Yaba. But the food delivery is almost beside the point. The actual bet is this: if you can get a Lagos user to open your app every time they want lunch, you've built something more valuable than a delivery business. You've built a daily habit. And a user with a daily habit is a user you can eventually ask to send money, buy airtime, pay bills, without having to earn their trust from scratch each time. That's the super app thesis. Food delivery as the opening move. Financial services as the destination. It's a sound idea. It's also the same idea that OPay, Gokada, and MAX all had at different points, and all eventually stepped back from, because the distance between "user who orders food" and "user who trusts you with their money" is longer and harder to close than the thesis assumes. The retention problem inside the super app model is specific. Food delivery builds frequency, but frequency alone doesn't build financial trust. A user can order from Swoop three times a week and still open a different app when they need to transfer money, because the mental category for "food app" and "money app" doesn't automatically collapse just because they live in the same interface. What closes that gap is something Chowdeck has been building quietly for four years, the kind of reliability that makes a user stop thinking about whether the app will work and just use it. That's not something $7.3 million buys directly. It accumulates through consistent delivery, through rider networks that hold up in the rain, through customer service that resolves the order that went wrong. Swoop is starting in Yaba, which is a sensible choice. Dense restaurants, users who already order online, infrastructure that's manageable. But Yaba is also where Chowdeck, Glovo, and FoodCourt already operate. The users Swoop actually needs to convert to make the super app thesis work, lower-income, cash-preferring, first-time digital consumers on the outskirts of Lagos, are not in Yaba. And those users are going to require a very different activation and trust-building approach than the ones already comfortable ordering food on their phones. Whether the habit Swoop builds in Yaba is the right foundation for the product they actually want to become is the question worth watching. Do you think food delivery can genuinely build the kind of daily trust that makes a Lagos user move their money through the same app, or does financial trust have to be earned on its own terms?

My first-ever hackathon was the Berkeley AI Hackathon 2026, and it turned out to be one of the most valuable learning experiences I've had. I had the opportunity to work alongside Edwin N. Ruiz-Rodriguez , cofounder of Swoop, a food delivery platform based in Africa that has raised over $7 million in funding, and Nicolas Vega , founder of AgenticIDE, who is building agentic infrastructure for AI-powered software development. Collaborating with founders and experienced AI engineers gave me valuable insight into how ambitious AI products are architected, developed, and brought to market. Together, we built an AI-powered Debate RPG where autonomous LLM agents act as collectible "monsters" inside a living RPG world. Players explore, collect debate agents, train their behavior, and battle enemy AI personas through judged argument rounds. Under the hood, this became a full-stack AI system powered by FastAPI, React, Vite, Phaser, WebSockets, Docker, Postgres, pgvector, Redis, and Ollama. We implemented retrieval-augmented memory, real-time battle streaming, autonomous agent behaviors, prompt optimization workflows, and latency-aware model routing. My biggest takeaway was that AI engineering is far more than calling an API. Building useful AI products requires robust systems for memory, validation, state management, streaming, reliability, and user experience. The model is only one part of a much larger architecture. Grateful for the opportunity to compete, learn from exceptional builders, and gain hands-on experience developing agentic systems and real-time AI applications. Excited to keep building AI-native products and pushing deeper into production-scale AI engineering. #ArtificialIntelligence #AIEngineering #GenerativeAI #Hackathon #FullStackDevelopment #GameDevelopment #LLM #MachineLearning
